data.title: Rich Parents' Don't Want Their Kids to Catch 'Affluenza.' How to Prevent It. — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Lorna Gray

At 3 a.m. in Amsterdam, my son called me with a problem. He and four friends had booked a hostel after graduating from high school, but one of the boys was under 18 and the group couldn't all stay there. My son wanted to know what to do, and I told him I was an ocean away and he would have to figure it out.

A few hours later, he called again to say the boys had solved the problem themselves, finding a hotel arrangement for the younger traveler while the others kept the hostel rooms they had already paid for. No parent called a concierge, a friend in Europe or the hotel manager. The young people assessed the situation, made trade-offs and moved on.

It is a small story, but it captures a larger challenge I see in affluent families. Parents work hard to give their children every opportunity, yet in doing so they can sometimes make life so seamless that young people lack opportunities to develop judgment for themselves.

What gets called "affluenza" is often treated as a character flaw, as though too much money inevitably produces a sense of entitlement or a lack of grit. That explanation is too simple. Money itself isn't the problem. The greater risk is that financial resources and parental intervention become so effective at solving problems that a young adult has too few chances to make decisions, weigh consequences and build confidence through experience.

Cerulli Associates projects that U.S. households will transfer $123.7 trillion between 2024 and 2048, with $105.3 trillion of that going to heirs. Advisors have spent a decade preparing the assets, but the open question is how much has been spent preparing the people who will receive them.

Developing self-sufficiency. Financial advisors can help change that pattern, particularly during the college years, when young adults begin managing money and taking on responsibilities that can prepare them for future stewardship.

Parents naturally want to protect their children, but protection and preparation aren't always the same thing. Pew Research Center's 2024 study of parents and young adults found an instructive gap in perception: 86% of parents of 18- to 34-year-olds said they did at least a fair amount to prepare their children to be independent adults, while only 66% of young adults agreed. The same study found that 59% of parents had given their young adult child financial help in the past year, and that only 45% of young adults considered themselves completely financially independent.

Parents, in other words, tend to grade their own preparation more generously than their children do, and the support itself is nearly universal. The lesson isn't that parents should cut off support at 18. It is that support should build capacity rather than replace it.

Here is how parents, often with help from financial advisors, can help:

Make money visible. Parents can fund college without handling every transaction, giving a student responsibility for agreed-upon expenses from a defined account or semester budget. An advisor could be the one to set the budget, size the reserve, and write down in advance what counts as a genuine emergency. That last piece matters most. A definition agreed in calm conditions is what allows a parent to hold the line at 3 a.m., and it gives the student a boundary they can actually see.

Establish spending rules. Families should also define and write down what they will support and what they won't automatically rescue. Health, safety and education may be nonnegotiable commitments, while discretionary overspending, missed deadlines and poor planning don't always require an immediate parental fix.

A missed train, an overdrawn budget or an apartment problem can require a young person to evaluate options, tolerate discomfort and make a decision. That is how judgment develops. An advisor can hold that list and refer back to it, which is considerably easier than asking a parent to hold it alone against a distressed phone call.

Help them find meaning. I have spent years working with high-achieving students who can perform exceptionally well within a structure created for them, yet struggle when asked what they value or what direction they would choose for themselves.

A 2026 report from Harvard Graduate School of Education's Making Caring Common project found that 51% of Gen Z adults ages 18 to 29 reported lacking meaning or purpose, or both. Young adults who felt needed and believed they made a positive difference in others' lives were much more likely to experience meaning or purpose. Seventy-nine percent said they wanted work that helps others or creates positive change.

Make them responsible. The intervention isn't a values conversation but a role. A young adult given something important to be responsible for, where other people depend on the outcome, is being handed the conditions the research associates with purpose. Advisors are already in the business of assigning responsibility. Family philanthropy, a junior role in a family entity, a defined piece of the family's giving budget with real authority attached, all of these are available.

Advisors are well positioned to help because they can serve as a neutral adult in emotionally loaded family conversations. Family meetings should not be limited to trusts, taxes and investment policy. They can also become a setting for progressively transferring responsibility and allowing young adults to participate as developing decision makers rather than simply as future beneficiaries.

The best measure of readiness for wealth isn't whether a young adult can recite the family balance sheet. It is whether they can exercise judgment, recover from mistakes, and handle an obligation that someone else is counting on.

Families already devote enormous attention to preparing assets for the next generation. The $105 trillion moving to heirs over the next two decades will land somewhere regardless of whether anyone is ready for it. Advisors can help ensure the next generation is prepared for the responsibility. Continuity depends not only on what a family transfers, but on who is ready to receive it.

Lorna Gray is the founder and president of Interface EDU, a college counseling and family advisory practice. Nearly 20 years of advising ultra-high-net-worth families led her to create Rising Generational Development, a discipline that prepares heirs to responsibly handle wealth by building the identity, motivation and judgment.

data.title: Airline Stocks Drop After FAA Temporarily Halts Flights — WSJ
data.description:
Airline stocks ticked lower this afternoon and fell further in postmarket trading following the Federal Aviation Administration's decision to halt flight departures nationwide.

The FAA cited extraordinary circumstances and safety concerns after air traffic control communications were disrupted. In afterhours trading, United Airlines stock fell 2.3%, Delta Air Lines was off 1% and American Airlines was down 1.8%.

This item is part of a Wall Street Journal live coverage event. The full stream can be found by searching P/WSJL (WSJ Live Coverage).

data.title: Sysco Declares Quarterly Dividend Payment
data.description:
HOUSTON, Nov. 13, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Sysco Corporation today announced that the Board of Directors declared a quarterly cash dividend of $0.55 per share, payable on January 29, 2027, to common stockholders of record at the close of business on January 8, 2027.

About Sysco

Sysco is the global leader in selling, marketing and distributing food and related products to customers who prepare meals away from home. This includes restaurants, healthcare and educational facilities, lodging establishments, entertainment venues, and more. Sysco operates 333 distribution centers, in 10 countries, with 75,000 colleagues serving approximately 670,000 customer locations. The company generated sales of more than $84 billion in fiscal year 2026 that ended June 27, 2026.

As the world’s largest food-away-from-home distributor, Sysco offers customized supply chain solutions, bespoke specialty product offerings, and culinary support to drive customers to innovate and optimize their operations. We act as a trusted business partner to our customers, helping them grow through our industry-leading portfolio that includes fresh produce, premium proteins, specialty products, sustainably focused items, equipment and supplies, and innovative culinary solutions.

For more information, visit www.sysco.com. For important news and key information for Sysco investors, visit the Investor Relations section of the company’s website at investors.sysco.com.
